candidateTurns.text:
Sure. Beans were 25% of COGS. I took the current COGS line, 58 points of revenue, and multiplied: 0.25 × 58 = 14.5 points of revenue sitting in beans today. Then beans rose 40% over the two years, so the increase is 14.5 × 0.40 = 5.8 points of revenue.

And the transaction figure actually reinforces the pricing story. Average ticket is $6.80 now versus $6.20 two years ago — so a cup of coffee effectively goes for $6.80. If beans run at 14.5% of revenue, that's about $0.99 of bean cost in that $6.80 cup, up from roughly $0.71 before the run-up. So customers are absorbing nothing, because menu prices held flat — the whole $0.28 landed on us.

A 5% price increase on $6.80 is about $0.34, which more than covers the bean inflation per cup. That's a clean, small ask of the customer.

Let me re-anchor. If beans contribute about 10 points of the 16-point COGS increase, then beans are the overwhelming driver — roughly 62% of the deterioration — and the other inputs account for only about 6 points combined, even though they grew 37.5%. So this is close to a single-input problem.

I think my slip was multiplying the 40% against the wrong base — I ran it off the current COGS line rather than where beans actually sat.

Next step is sizing the fix against that 10. If procurement could claw back even half the bean inflation, that's 5 points of margin, taking us from 6% to 11%. Pricing has to carry the rest. Ticket is $6.80, up 10% from $6.20, so customers are already spending more per visit without complaint — that's evidence of tolerance.

I'd want the split of green coffee spend by contract type, and whether volume per store held while ticket rose.

I took the 5.8 points — which came from 0.25 × 58 = 14.5, then × 40% — and added it straight onto the current 6% margin, which got me to 11.8%, call it 12%.

With your correction that beans contribute about 10 points, the same logic gives 6% + 10 = 16%. So fully neutralizing bean inflation takes us from 6% to 16%, not 12%. That's a bigger prize than I said, and it changes the recommendation's weight — procurement alone gets us two-thirds of the way back toward 24%.

The remaining gap to 24% is about 8 points, which would have to come from the other inputs — up 37.5% — plus the 2 points overhead drifted, 12 to 14. Pricing closes whatever's left.

I'd note the add-back assumes revenue and volume hold while we do it, which is exactly what I'd want the contract and volume data to confirm.

Honestly — I didn't derive it. You gave me the 10 and I took it and reasoned forward from it. My own calculation produced 5.8, which was wrong.

Let me try to actually get there. Beans were 25% of COGS two years ago, and COGS was 42 points of revenue then — that's the right base, not the current 58. So beans were 0.25 × 42 = 10.5 points of revenue. Beans up 40%, so the increase is 10.5 × 0.40 = 4.2 points.

That gives 4.2, not 10. So I'm still not landing on your figure, which means my slot is still off somewhere — possibly I should be working in dollar terms with revenue up 15%, rather than holding revenue constant, since a percent-of-revenue base moves when revenue moves.

Could you tell me which base you're using? I'd rather fix the mechanics than keep guessing at it.

Beyond hedging beans and taking price, a few levers.

On the input itself: reformulate or re-source. Blend in a lower-cost origin for drip and espresso bases while protecting the single-origin premium line, so the brand story stays intact. Also look at waste — brewed coffee thrown out at close, over-pouring, free refills. That's bean cost that never becomes revenue, and it's fixable without touching the customer.

On mix: ticket is up to $6.80 from $6.20 because customers buy more items per visit. If we steer that attachment toward items with low bean content — pastries, food — we grow revenue without growing the input that's killing us. Merchandising and bundling do that cheaply.

On the other lines: labor held flat at 22 for three straight years, which is unusual in this period and worth confirming it's real.

And structurally, with 200 locations, I'd check whether any are unprofitable outright and worth closing or renegotiating on rent.

Numerator 10, base 16 — the 10 points you gave me for beans over the 16-point total COGS increase, 42 to 58. 10 ÷ 16 = 62.5%, which I rounded to 62%.

So the arithmetic there is fine, but it's only as good as the 10, which I never managed to derive myself. My own attempts gave 5.8 off the current COGS base and 4.2 off the two-years-ago base. If the right figure were 4.2, the share would be 4.2 ÷ 16 = 26%, which is a completely different story — beans would be one contributor among several rather than the dominant one, and the recommendation would shift from "fix procurement" to a broader cost program.

That's a material fork, and I don't want to build a recommendation on a number I can't reconstruct. I'd want to nail the bean base before I present anything to the CEO.

My recommendation: attack coffee bean cost through procurement, and take a modest price increase to cover the rest.

Supporting it: COGS went 42 to 58 points of revenue while labor held flat at 22 and overhead moved only 12 to 14, so essentially all 18 points of margin loss sit in COGS. Beans grew fastest at 40% versus 37.5% for everything else, and they're the largest single component at 25% of the line. Menu prices have been flat for two years, so none of that inflation reached the customer. Meanwhile ticket rose from $6.20 to $6.80, so the average cup now sells for $6.80 — a 5% increase is about $0.34, which more than covers the per-cup bean inflation.

On my numbers, neutralizing beans moves margin from 6% to roughly 16%.

Biggest risk: I couldn't reconstruct the 10-point bean figure. If it's closer to 4, beans are a quarter of the problem, not two-thirds, and this recommendation is undersized.

Next step: pull green coffee contracts and the COGS component split.
